qs.q: A patient with acute rheumatic fever develops Sydenham's chorea. What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism?
o: Direct bacterial invasion of the central nervous
Molecular mimicry affecting basal ganglia neurons
Toxin-mediated damage to the cerebral cortex region
Immune complex deposition in the brain vasculature
qs.e: Sydenham's chorea results from molecular mimicry where antibodies cross-react with brain tissue.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Bacteriology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 14-year-old girl diagnosed with Sydenham chorea is monitored for long-term complications. What is the approximate percentage of such patients who eventually develop chronic rheumatic valve disease?
o: Less than 5 percent of affected patients
qs.e: While neurological symptoms of chorea often resolve spontaneously, approximately one-quarter of these patients eventually develop chronic rheumatic heart disease. This proportion underscores the need for continued cardiovascular surveillance.

qs.q: During sleep, what typically happens to the abnormal involuntary movements seen in a patient with Sydenham's chorea?
o: They transform into generalized tonic-clonic seizures
They worsen significantly due to lack of cortical control
They remain unchanged throughout the night
qs.e: Sydenham's chorea is characterized by sudden aimless movements, but these symptoms subside during sleep. The onset is gradual and can be accompanied by emotional instability.

qs.q: Which of the following drugs is recommended for treating severe cases of Sydenham's chorea?
qs.e: Severe Sydenham's chorea is managed with anticonvulsants or agents like phenobarbitone or haloperidol. Mild cases require bed rest and stress avoidance.

ai.title: Sydenham Chorea
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Sydenham chorea is a post‑streptococcal movement disorder seen in children and adolescents, often part of acute rheumatic fever. It presents with involuntary, irregular movements and may coexist with carditis or arthritis.

sections.p: A hyperkinetic movement disorder caused by autoimmune basal ganglia injury after group A streptococcal infection, diagnosed by clinical features and evidence of recent streptococcal exposure.
b: Irregular, non‑rhythmic, purposeless movements of limbs, face, or trunk
Excludes other causes of chorea (e.g., Huntington disease, drug‑induced)
Positive streptococcal serology (ASO or anti‑DNAse B) supports diagnosis

sections.p: Severity is graded by functional impact: mild (only observable by examiner), moderate (interferes with daily tasks), severe (causes falls, inability to feed).
b: Mild – movements limited to hands, no functional loss
Moderate – difficulty with writing, dressing, feeding
Severe – frequent falls, inability to perform self‑care

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the most common trigger is recent untreated streptococcal pharyngitis leading to acute rheumatic fever.
b: Post‑streptococcal (acute rheumatic fever) – most frequent
Systemic lupus erythematosus – consider if other SLE features present
Drug‑induced (antipsychotics, levodopa) – rare in this age group
Metabolic (hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia) – rule out if systemic signs

sections.p: Patients develop sudden onset of jerky, dance‑like movements that worsen with stress and improve with rest; speech may become slurred, and emotional lability is common.
b: Random, flowing movements of hands, feet, face
Facial grimacing, tongue protrusion, dysarthria
Emotional irritability, anxiety, insomnia

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm recent streptococcal infection and assess for associated rheumatic fever complications.

t.b: Evidence of recent GAS infection; elevated titre supports post‑streptococcal aetiology
Detects carditis (valvular regurgitation, pericardial effusion); presence changes management
Looks for anemia or leukocytosis; may suggest concurrent infection
Exclude hyperthyroidism as an alternative cause of chorea

t.a: If echocardiography unavailable – bedside cardiac exam
t.b: Detect murmurs, signs of heart failure; guides urgency of referral

sections.p: Complications arise from severe motor impairment, associated carditis, or secondary injuries.
b: Sudden worsening of chorea causing falls or aspiration
New or worsening murmur, dyspnoea, peripheral edema (carditis)
Psychiatric decompensation – severe anxiety or depression

sections.p: Treat the underlying autoimmune process, control movements, and monitor cardiac involvement.
b: Penicillin prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin G IM every 3‑4 weeks) to eradicate residual GAS and prevent recurrence
Haloperidol (low dose) for severe, disabling chorea – chosen for rapid control; avoid high doses due to extrapyramidal risk
Sodium valproate or carbamazepine as alternatives when haloperidol contraindicated (e.g., severe sedation risk)
Supportive physiotherapy and a calm environment to reduce stimulus‑induced worsening

sections.p: Long‑term secondary prophylaxis and periodic cardiac review are essential.
b: Continue penicillin prophylaxis for at least 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer
Repeat echocardiography every 6‑12 months to monitor for late carditis
Educate family on early signs of streptococcal infection and importance of treatment

sections.p: Conditions that produce involuntary movements can mimic Sydenham chorea.
b: Huntington disease – progressive, family history, cognitive decline
Drug‑induced chorea – temporal relation to neuroleptic or levodopa use
Wilson disease – hepatic signs, Kayser‑Fleischer rings

sections.p: Serology and imaging may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal ASO does not exclude recent infection if test performed > 6 weeks after onset
Mild valvular regurgitation can be missed on low‑resolution echo; careful auscultation is vital

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe worsening of movements with loss of balance
New cardiac murmur, dyspnoea, or peripheral oedema
Signs of aspiration or inability to swallow

faq.q: Why does Sydenham chorea improve with rest?
faq.a: Stress and emotional excitement increase basal‑ganglia excitability; rest reduces sympathetic drive and lessens movements.

faq.q: Can the chorea recur after treatment?
faq.a: Recurrence is possible if secondary penicillin prophylaxis is stopped prematurely or a new streptococcal infection occurs.
Low‑dose haloperidol is used for severe cases; monitor for extrapyramidal side‑effects and limit duration.

exam: A 12‑year‑old presents with involuntary hand movements and a recent sore throat – what is your next diagnostic step? — Check ASO/anti‑DNAse B and perform bedside cardiac exam to assess for rheumatic fever.
How would you differentiate Sydenham chorea from Huntington disease in a teenager? — Emphasise acute onset after GAS infection, presence of carditis, and lack of family history or cognitive decline.
A patient with severe chorea cannot feed herself – which medication would you start and why? — Low‑dose haloperidol for rapid control; avoid high doses due to extrapyramidal risk.
What is the rationale for long‑term penicillin prophylaxis in Sydenham chorea? — Prevents recurrent GAS infection and subsequent rheumatic fever recurrences that could worsen cardiac disease.
If echocardiography is unavailable, how do you assess for carditis? — Perform thorough cardiac auscultation for murmurs, assess for signs of heart failure, and refer urgently if abnormal.
A child on valproate develops rash and liver enzymes rise – what is your next step? — Stop valproate, consider switching to haloperidol or carbamazepine, and monitor hepatic function.
Explain why a normal ASO titre does not rule out Sydenham chorea. — ASO peaks 3‑5 weeks after infection and may normalize; clinical context and other serology (anti‑DNAse B) are needed.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate hospital admission? — New cardiac murmur with dyspnoea or peripheral oedema indicating possible acute carditis.
